paragraphs: In the spring of the twenty-seventh year of Jianyuan, the Ba River thawed. Sunlight mottled the thin ice. A boatman pushed with his long pole, overturning a sheet of it and exposing the deep green water below. After the morning audience, Fu Jian did not return to the palace. As his carriage left the city, he ordered his guards to stop before a courier granary and went to touch the newly replaced wooden bar on its door.
Ink on the wood recorded the repair date as the previous year. The writing was fresh, but the iron ring around the lock was badly worn.
“What is Your Majesty looking at?” a guard asked.
“The money and grain for these repairs were allotted last year. The bar was replaced this year.”
Fu Rong came up from behind. “Imperial Brother, must you investigate even this yourself?”
“I was passing and saw it.”
“You chose to look. There are dozens more granaries in Luoyang. At this rate you may not be back by summer.”
Fu Jian smiled, but when he climbed into the carriage he steadied himself on the shaft. Fu Rong noticed and said nothing.

Four years before, when the great flood struck Hebei, granaries in Guanzhong, Henei, and Luoyang had all sent grain north. After the waters subsided, the Secretariat examined the vouchers month by month, but one group of old accounts only became more tangled. The men who had hauled the grain swore that the full amounts reached Ye; ferry stations along the way reported boats returning empty. One granary officer recorded a loss of three hundred shi; the commandery office issued replacement vouchers for five hundred. Every paper bore a seal. Yet between those seals no one could account for all the grain.

Fu Jian inspected Luoyang with more than a thousand imperial guards. There was no triumphal procession. Along the road he heard only reports on stores, river transport, and conscript labor. His clerks had prepared stacks of canal-repair plans, but he asked first about granary deficits. The next day he opened an old granary west of the city.

As the doors swung wide, a sour, moldy smell struck them. The accounts called for twenty thousand shi of millet, but sacks filled scarcely half the main storehouse. The upper layers were neatly arranged; beneath them lay damp sand and rotten wheat. A sack gnawed through by rats showed bright golden millet at the mouth. Two layers lower, the grain turned black and gray with age.
The granary superintendent knelt at the entrance, sweat beading at his temples.
“The emergency relief for Hebei was issued first and reconciled afterward.”

Fu Jian asked for three vouchers. Two carried the signatures of relief commissioners and local granary seals. The third bore only the vermilion mark of a granary clerk. The name of the colonel on it could not be found in the Hebei military rolls consulted by the accompanying Central Army Office officer.
“Who collected it?”
“An officer from Ye.”
“What proof did you have that he was an officer?”
“He wore a military uniform and carried a handwritten order.”
“Where is the order?”
“He said he had to take it back to report.”

Fu Jian turned the voucher over. The paper fibers were old, but the seal paste was fresh; strokes in the date had been altered. He did not shout in anger. Instead he asked the superintendent to rise and point out, on the map, the courier route by which the officer had entered the city. At the third location, the man named a ferry crossing that had been washed away in the flood itself.
Fu Rong saw his brother fold the voucher and slip it into his sleeve. He knew this would end in more than a reprimand.

The censors questioned granary guards, cart drivers, and shop assistants separately. Three days later they discovered that the supposed colonel from Hebei was a steward in a Luoyang salt merchant’s household. He had taken new grain out, then bought old millet mixed with sand outside the city to replace it. Over several months, the vouchers had passed through more than one granary office. The accompanying clerks compared dates of departure and arrival with cart totals. Almost forty thousand shi were missing, although much of that figure still required verification.

Fu Jian ordered the Secretariat to fill the relief shortfall from other granaries first; the pursuit of thieves must not interrupt deliveries to the villages. He then directed the censors to seal the merchant family’s account books and investigate the granary superintendent and prefect separately. Someone proposed arresting every man in the granary office.

“Someone must guard the doors, and someone must write the records,” Fu Jian said. “Question each person through whose hands a false voucher passed. Even the man who saw an empty cart yet reported it full must have a chance to speak. Bind them all today, and who will send grain to the counties tomorrow?”

An elderly minister quietly urged severe punishment for officials who had deceived their sovereign, to warn the rest. Fu Jian merely waved him off and told someone to take him to see the empty storehouse.

Rain fell on Luoyang on the fifth day. After breathing the damp air of the granaries, Fu Jian coughed so badly he could not sleep. Fu Rong sent a physician, who said the chill had not left his body and advised him against going out in the rain. He agreed readily, then proposed visiting the river granary the next morning.

A section of the river granary’s wharf had collapsed in the previous spring floods. Old planks had been laid as a temporary landing. A grain boat from Henei lay stranded in shallow water. More than twenty laborers had removed their shoes and stood barefoot in the icy current, carrying sacks ashore along a swaying gangplank. Fu Jian watched from beneath a rain cloak for a long time.

Halfway across, a young man bearing a sack slipped and fell partly into the water. Others lunged to pull him back, but most of the grain sack was soaked. Seeing Fu Jian, the transport officer panicked and began by berating the laborer. He ordered a clerk to record the loss and deduct fifteen days' labor pay.
“How much does he earn in a day?” Fu Jian asked.
“Twenty coins. If the wet grain spoils, he must repay three hundred.”
“How much has spoiled?”
The river officer could not say.
“Spread it out to dry first, then calculate the loss. And give him dry clothes.”

Fu Jian stepped onto the gangplank, leaving slick pools of water under his shoes. Nails had worked loose where the planks met. If the boat shifted any farther, the entire section would overturn into the river.
“Has this been repaired?”
“The craftsmen were moved to the granary east of the city.”
“How long ago?”
“Seventeen days.”
“It may take seventeen days to repair a granary, but surely not to mend one plank.”

Fu Rong hurried onto the gangplank to support him. He was about to laugh and chide his brother for attending to every minor affair when the weight in his hands suddenly sagged. Fu Jian covered his mouth and coughed twice. A little dark red showed between his fingers. Fu Rong’s smile vanished.
“Back to the temporary palace.”

Fu Jian was still looking at the gangplank submerged in the water and wanted to say something more, but his chest abruptly tightened. Fu Rong did not wait for another command. He ordered the procession withdrawn.

High fever came that night. The palace physicians felt his pulse and at first called it a chill that had reached the lungs. They prepared medicinal broth. At dawn he was worse. Phlegm rattled deep in Fu Jian’s chest. When awake he asked for water, only to cough after half a mouthful. Several times he tried to rise; when his feet reached the floor, he could not stand steadily.
Fu Rong moved the stacks of granary books from the bedside to an outer room. Fu Jian woke in the night and reached toward the papers on the table, but his fingers found only a thin blanket.
“The accounts?”
“Being examined.”
“By whom?”
“The censors, the Secretariat, and me.”
“You know how to audit granary accounts now?”
“No. I watch them do it. If anyone cheats me, I’ll send him and the accounts to Chang’an together.”
Fu Jian’s lips moved in something like a smile. Fu Rong leaned closer and found his forehead burning. The trace of humor froze on his own face.
“Brother, I’ll summon the Crown Prince.”
“Don’t bring him here.”
“You are gravely ill.”
“If he comes, who will govern the court?”
Fu Rong was struck silent.
“Tell him the truth,” Fu Jian continued. “Tell Chang’an they are not to call it merely a chill. If I cannot attend to affairs, let him supervise the government under the established rules.”
Fu Rong pressed his lips together. “We do not yet know the cause of the illness. If rumors spread that you have died—”
“If I am not dead, write that I am not dead. If anything changes after tonight, report it again.”

Fu Rong looked at him. In their youth his elder brother had always decided quickly, while Fu Rong considered the roads of retreat. Now his brother lay in bed and still thought first about what people a thousand leagues away must do.
“I’m afraid that when the news reaches them, each faction will move its troops,” Fu Rong said quietly.
“The more you fear it, the more clearly they must know who has the authority to move troops.”

That day three dispatches bearing identical wording left the temporary palace: the Heavenly King had developed a high fever while inspecting granaries and could not presently conduct affairs; the Crown Prince would supervise the government according to precedent; the Secretariat would continue its work; provincial armies were to remain at their assigned defenses and not cross garrison boundaries on the pretext of guarding the sovereign; troop movements still required verification of all three seals. The imperial seal remained at the Luoyang residence, its keys divided between Fu Rong and the official seal keeper accompanying the court, with a copy of the sealing record preserved separately. Couriers rode out through the eastern gate, oilcloth tied around their messages against the rain.

In the streets of Luoyang, word first spread that the Heavenly King was dying. Someone saw the physicians change medicine pots several times in a night and announced that a coffin was being prepared. Someone else saw white cloth being sewn at the residence and claimed funeral banners were ready. Later the cloth was used to replace the sickroom curtains, while the carpenters had been repairing the river granary’s sluice gate. No one wanted to hear the explanations.

When the news reached Chang’an, Fu Hong was reviewing land deeds from Hebei after the flood. A rejected petition lay on his desk, disputing a ditch whose course had changed in a flash flood. At the sound of the eastern courier’s hooves in the courtyard, the officials of the Secretariat stopped writing.
The Crown Prince read the dispatch without speaking. The clerk standing below the steps saw his thumb press down the corner of the paper, the knuckles whitening by degrees.
“When was it sent?”
“Yesterday, in the late afternoon.”
“Is my uncle at the residence?”
“The Duke of Yangping is guarding it. The imperial seal has been secured.”
“How often has my father woken?”
“He has regained consciousness at intervals, even during the worst of the illness. The latest urgent dispatch follows.”

Fu Hong ordered the courier taken out, fed, and given rest. Only then did he command the bell for council to be struck. He neither sealed the palace gates nor allowed attendants to obstruct ministers coming to ask questions. In Taiji Hall the throne stood empty. He placed a mat below it and read the Luoyang dispatch word for word to the assembled ministers.

Whispers passed through the hall. Some members of the imperial clan asked whether the king had been poisoned; others proposed sending princes with guards to protect him. The finance officers feared merchants would hoard grain; the military administrators feared frontier garrisons would seize the moment to move troops. Fu Hong heard them all, then issued orders one by one. Only three representatives of the imperial clan could travel in successive groups to tend the patient at Luoyang, taking no private soldiers. Chang’an’s official markets would open as usual the next day. More millet would be issued from public stores, with limits per household so wealthy families could not buy everything. The city gates would open and close on schedule, and patrols would continue their normal checks.
Only after issuing the orders did he notice an elderly prince who had said nothing. The old man rose on his staff and asked, “Is Your Highness truly not afraid?”

“I am afraid,” Fu Hong said. “Afraid that the next report from Luoyang will say my father will never wake. And afraid that before such a report arrives, someone will have arranged his funeral for us.”
The old prince leaned on his staff and argued no further.

After the council, Murong Chui remained. Years had passed since he returned from reporting his flood-relief work in Hebei; his hair and beard were whiter, but he still wore his unmistakable black outer robe. Fu Hong drew out two verified land deeds from Ye and handed them to him.
“Grand Commandant, both deeds claim the same piece of land. Whoever hears the news first could use it to recruit soldiers.”
Murong Chui examined them. “Old estate accounts again.”
“What will Hebei do when it hears my father is gravely ill?”
“Some will burn incense, some will drink wine, and some will dig out the old Yan coins that have been hidden away for years.”
“Will they raise troops?”

“That depends first on whether the granary doors in Ye continue to open. If they do, people have plenty to occupy them. If you dismiss the Xianbei officials before anything happens, you will be showing the disaffected which road to take.”

Fu Hong considered this, then ordered the Secretariat to publish the names of serving officials in Hebei and a directive to maintain grain supply from the ever-normal granaries. No one was to be abruptly replaced merely because of his family name. He asked Murong Chui to travel north as an envoy of the Qin court to reassure the region, without granting him a separate military command in Hebei.
Murong Chui stood. “You would send me without an army?”
“You will have the government’s courier guards. Troops along the road will remain under their present commanders.”

Murong Chui looked at the prince. He remembered a night outside Chengming Hall more than twenty years before, when tiger tallies had been taken one by one from the belts of the generals. Fu Jian could not speak for himself now. Yet Fu Hong was still willing to send Murong Chui to Hebei without using the occasion to give him an army beholden solely to the Murong house.
“I’ll go.”
He reached the doorway, then turned back. “And there is Xiangyang.”
Fu Hong looked up.
“Once your elder brother Fu Pi hears that Luoyang is in crisis, he will ask to bring troops back. His intentions may be good, but everyone around him is hoping he will arrive with soldiers.”

Fu Hong neither agreed nor disagreed. He had a clerk bring the military reports from Xiangyang for the previous three months. After reading them for a while, he set aside the words he had first drafted, “No army may return north,” and took a new sheet to write privately to his brother. He described their father’s illness and conditions in Chang’an, asked Fu Pi to hold his city, and said he could petition to visit their father.

Before the private letter left Chang’an, grain prices had risen in the southern market. A rice shop changed its posted prices twice in half a day. An old woman in front of a public granary cart cupped copper coins in her sleeve and tugged at a worker. “My grandson must eat tomorrow morning too. If you give us grain today, will there be any tomorrow?”

Sweating heavily, the worker showed her a voucher bearing the public granary seal, but she could not read. A cloth seller standing nearby read it aloud: deliveries would continue as normal for three days. She asked only, “Who sealed it?”
“The Secretariat.”
“The Crown Prince?”
“Yes.”

The woman drew the coins tighter into her sleeve and waited for her measure of grain, still looking back toward the street from time to time. She returned the next day. The public granary cart duly arrived, and the line was a little shorter.

At least one urgent courier came from Luoyang every day. If rain delayed one by two hours, the ministers filled the Secretariat courtyard waiting. The third report said Fu Jian lay unresponsive in a deep sleep, though his pulse continued, and Fu Rong remained at the residence. Fu Hong unfolded the report before them all, ordered copies made, and sent them to the ancestral temple and every military office. Someone warned that such openness might alarm the people. He replied, “Tonight someone will say my father is dead. If there is no genuine dispatch in the morning, another will come bearing a false one.”

The envoy from Xiangyang arrived that afternoon. Fu Pi’s memorial first asked after their father’s illness, then requested permission to lead three thousand household troops to the capital to tend him and assist the Crown Prince in keeping the military administration stable. His signature at the end was so forceful that the ink nearly bled through the paper. Some princes urged consent, saying it was proper for brothers to visit an ailing father. A veteran of the Central Army Office who had known Fu Pi for years also felt three thousand mounted guards were no more than a protective escort.

Fu Hong read the memorial and asked first how many state courier stations and garrisons lay between Xiangyang and Luoyang. The officials gave him the figures; no major bandit danger had been reported along the nearest roads. He therefore permitted Fu Pi himself to return along the courier route with a hundred attendants, while the Xiangyang garrison remained at its post. The reply said that if Fu Pi wished to go directly to Luoyang to attend the sickbed, the temporary palace could authorize the visit first; he must not assemble troops on his own in Guanzhong.

The general responsible for the seal hesitated a long time. An old Di officer who had campaigned with Fu Pi at Xiangyang, he looked up. “If Your Highness fears the troops, write that you fear them. Why place such limits on your own elder brother?”
Fu Hong looked at him. “Do you believe people in the city would feel safe if my brother arrived with three thousand men?”
“He would cause no disorder.”

“Then please put that judgment in the verification column, General, and sign your name. If you believe three thousand guards present no danger, state the military evidence on which you rely. Neither you nor I need discharge our duty with nothing more than a claim that we trust him or distrust him.”

The seal general took up his brush. Candlelight shone on his graying hair. After a long while he wrote, “No military threat reported along the route; an escort of one hundred is sufficient,” signed, and affixed the Central Army seal. The Secretariat then countersigned. The request for three thousand men to enter the capital was returned for amendment through the regular process.

After the court dispersed, Fu Hong remained on the mat below the empty throne. In one evening he had both allowed his brother to visit their father and kept his brother’s troops at Xiangyang. The work was done, but he remembered a rainy night at Wei Bridge many years before, when his father had pressed a hand against Fu Hong’s wounded cheek and said that some decisions, even when they were right, would bring no cheers.

Another day passed, and a small wooden box arrived from Luoyang. Inside were the papers from the river-granary case that Fu Jian had examined before his collapse. A dried, black drop of blood marked one corner. On the last page he had written half a line: “A river laborer who falls into the water and damages grain must not have his labor pay...” The brush had stopped there. A short note from Fu Rong accompanied it, only two sentences: The imperial seal remains secure. His Majesty has not awakened. No disturbance in Luoyang.

Fu Hong put the papers away. He did not complete the unfinished line for his father. Instead he issued a reply: Every office in Chang’an remains open. No garrison has moved. No disturbance in Chang’an.

That night in the temporary palace at Luoyang, Fu Rong had gone two nights without sleep. The physicians changed Fu Jian’s medicine, lifting his covers with the delicacy of men afraid of shattering something. The Heavenly King’s breathing grew heavy, then faint; phlegm still rattled deep in his chest. After a fit of feverish coughing, his lips moved.
Fu Rong leaned closer. He thought he heard the word “seal.”
“All locked away,” Fu Rong whispered. “The three offices have theirs. Everyone is at his post.”
Fu Jian did not wake.

Outside, the rain stopped. The watchman at Luoyang’s granary sounded the fourth watch as usual. The imperial seal lay untouched in its box at the temporary palace; no one opened it under cover of darkness. A thousand leagues away, the throne in Chang’an remained empty, but the lamps of the Secretariat burned from midnight until dawn.

At daybreak a register reviewing land deeds arrived from Ye at the household office. A young clerk checked the dates and seals and placed it in its proper wooden compartment. He did not know whether the Heavenly King would awaken that day. Neither did the courier who had delivered it. When their exchange of papers was complete, each went off to eat breakfast.
